title: Abusive supervision: distinguishing silence, withdrawal, and harmful workplace behavior
question: Is earlier perceived abusive supervision associated with later defensive silence, withdrawal and counterproductive behaviour, rated by different sources?

documents.text:
# Abusive supervision: distinguishing silence, withdrawal, and harmful workplace behavior

Narrative review draft (v2, full-text appraised) · not submission-ready · 9 October 2026

## Review question

Which mechanisms and outcomes are separated in research on abusive supervision?

Focus confirmed by the author on 9 October 2026 ([decisions](question-decisions.md)).

## Evidence base and method

**Source set.** All 74 PDFs in the author's curated reference folder for this paper (`Paper 9 Oct 2024/References/1ASL`) were identified against Crossref. Each identity required the article's own DOI or title on its first pages, and every record was checked for Crossref retraction and correction notices. This is a curated collection, not a systematic database search, so the conclusions below describe this collection. They are not a census of the field.

**Screening.** Records were included when employee-perceived abusive supervision was the exposure and at least one subordinate or team outcome was tested. 54 were included and 20 excluded: 8 studied antecedents of abuse, 3 studied supervisors' reactions to their own abuse, 3 tested abuse only as a moderator, 4 were non-empirical and 2 were off-topic. Reasons are recorded per record in `screening.json`.

**Extraction.** For each included study the design, sample, abuse measure, outcomes, who rated each outcome, mechanisms, supported and unsupported paths, and stated limitations were taken from the full text. Every quoted result carries its PDF page (`extraction.json`, [evidence table](#evidence-table)). Fields the passages read did not establish are left blank rather than inferred.

**Integrity checks.** No included record carries a Crossref retraction. One has a Crossref-listed correction [R1] and one a publisher corrigendum limited to author affiliations [R2]. Five studies report numbers that are internally inconsistent or implausible [R3, R4, R5], or claims their own analyses cannot support [R6, R7]. This review uses those studies only for design-level observations and cites none of their coefficients.

## What the collection shows

### 1. The three outcome families rest on unequal evidence

The question assumes silence, withdrawal and harm can be told apart. The collection measures them very differently:

| Outcome family | Outcome measures | Rated by the employee | Rated by someone else |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Citizenship, performance, creativity, learning | 21 | 7 | 12 (11 supervisor, 1 official record); 2 mixed or unclear |
| Harmful behaviour (CWB, deviance, aggression, retaliation) | 17 | 10 | 2 confirmed independent (1 supervisor, 1 official record); 5 mixed or unclear |
| Withdrawal (turnover intention, job search, psychological withdrawal) | 15 | 14 | 1 (supervisor) |
| Silence and withholding (silence, voice, knowledge hiding, feedback seeking) | 13 | 10 | 2 (supervisor); 1 unclear |
| Well-being and attitudes | 19 | 19 | 0 |

*Counts are outcome measures, not studies. One study can contribute several.*

Independent ratings are concentrated in citizenship and performance. For withdrawal, silence and most harmful behaviour, the person reporting the abuse also reports the outcome. Shared method variance therefore cannot be ruled out as part of any difference between the families. A claim that abuse "predicts silence more than withdrawal" would compare two self-reports with each other, not two behaviours.

The exceptions show what independent measurement adds:

- Team leaders rated subordinates' withdrawal at a later wave than the abuse report, and an indirect path through shame remained (ab = 0.02, 95% CI [0.01, 0.07]) [R8, PDF p6].
- In professional basketball, coder-rated coach abuse predicted officials' records of technical fouls and a decline in player efficiency over careers [R9, PDF pp22–23]. The setting limits how far this generalises.
- Supervisors rated two withholding outcomes, feedback seeking [R10] and knowledge sharing [R11], and miners' safety behaviour [R12].

### 2. "Silence" is several different behaviours

The silence-type studies measure at least six constructs:

- defensive silence, driven by fear [R13]
- fear-based silence [R4]
- reduced voice [R14, R15]
- knowledge hiding, split by one study into evasive hiding, playing dumb and rationalized hiding [R16]
- reduced feedback seeking [R10]
- facades of conformity [R17]

They are proposed to run through different mechanisms: fear [R13], psychological safety [R18], psychological contract breach [R19], organization-based self-esteem [R10] and emotional exhaustion [R15]. Only one study pits abuse against a competing supervisor behaviour for the same withholding outcomes: supervisors' own knowledge hiding predicted employees' hiding about 2.5 times more strongly than abusive supervision did [R16, abstract]. Collapsing these constructs into one "silence" outcome would hide such differences.

One finding runs against the others. In an Indian academic sample, abuse was reported to *reduce* knowledge hiding [R20, abstract and PDF p14]. It comes from a single cross-sectional study and needs replication before it is interpreted.

### 3. Harmful behaviour is separated by target

Harm studies distinguish targets: the supervisor [R3, R21], the organization [R22, R3], co-workers or other people [R23], customers [R24] and family members at home [R2]. Retaliation was also split by intensity, with in-kind aggression and escalated violence measured separately at later waves [R21]. Abuse also spreads sideways: it was associated with incivility from co-workers [R25] and, in an experiment and field study, with co-workers ostracising the victim [R26].

A team-level study links team abusive supervision to team resistance to change through distrust of the supervisor [R27]. Its source of ratings was not established in the passages read.

### 4. Mechanisms: justice and stress paths explain different outcomes

The one meta-analysis in the collection (427 primary studies) compares two explanations at once [R28]:

- **For citizenship, the justice path dominated.** The indirect effect through organizational justice was B = –.16 [–.17, –.15], and the direct effect became non-significant (B = –.02, p = .390) [PDF p12]. The indirect effect through work stress was smaller (B = –.03) [PDF p13], and the two differed significantly (ΔB = .13) [PDF p13].
- **For counterproductive behaviour, the stress path was the larger.** The indirect effect through stress was B = .07 [.06, .08], compared with B = .03 through justice [PDF p13]. The difference was significant (ΔB = .04) [PDF p14].
- **National masculinity** strengthened the abuse–CWB relation (B = .72, p = .001) but not the abuse–OCB relation (p = .748) [PDF p14].

This supports the review's premise that one generic "reaction to abuse" mechanism is not enough. The pooled correlations come mostly from cross-sectional primary studies, so these paths are associations, not causal effects.

In the primary studies, a motivation path (lower work engagement) linked abuse to supervisor-rated performance more strongly than a health path (emotional exhaustion) [R29, abstract]. Daily data showed engagement carrying the abuse–citizenship relation within persons [R14, abstract; PDF pp8–11]. Some proposed mechanisms failed: performance-promotion attributions were not related to abuse (p = .82) [R30, PDF p6], and psychological safety did not predict creativity [R31, PDF p10].

### 5. Abuse itself is not one thing

Several studies treat the exposure as having structure, a point the review question did not anticipate:

- Overt (active-aggressive) and covert (passive-aggressive) abuse correlated only r = .412 [R32, PDF p8] and were proposed to relate differently to learning behaviour.
- Being abused more or less than one's teammates (differentiation) predicted distress and quit intentions through insecure group attachment. Its predicted link to supervisor-rated unethical behaviour through attachment anxiety was not supported (95% CI [–0.01, 0.04]) [R33, PDF p13].
- Less variability of abuse within a group strengthened its negative relation to supervisor-rated performance and citizenship [R34, abstract].

A final review should treat the form and distribution of abuse as part of the exposure, not average it into one score.

### 6. Direction of causation is unresolved in this collection

Abuse is usually modelled as the cause. Two included studies point the other way. Employees lower in core self-evaluations reported receiving more abuse, which then predicted their deviance [R23]. In a three-study design, defensive silence was examined as a predictor of *later* abuse [R13]. The excluded antecedent studies also link subordinate performance to subsequent abuse (`screening.json`, idx 52).

Only 4 included studies use experimental or scenario manipulation [R35, R1, R36, R26]. Scenarios fix the direction of effect but raise external-validity concerns, as one study acknowledges [R1, PDF p8]. Most of the rest are cross-sectional (about 15) or multi-wave surveys (about 26), and multi-wave timing does not establish causation.

## Conclusions this collection supports

1. Silence, withdrawal and harm are measured as separate constructs in this literature, but **the evidence that they are separate behaviours is weak**. Most withdrawal, silence and harm outcomes share a reporter with the abuse measure.
2. Within families, the meaningful separations are by **target** (supervisor, organization, others, family) and by **behaviour type** (fearful silence vs. knowledge hiding vs. reduced feedback seeking). These finer distinctions are better supported than the three-way split.
3. **Justice and stress mechanisms explain different outcomes**: justice for citizenship, stress for counterproductive behaviour. This rests on one meta-analysis of mostly cross-sectional data.
4. Abuse should be treated as **multidimensional**: overt vs. covert, differentiated within groups, and varying.

## Limits of this review

- One curated folder: no database search, no grey literature, no non-English sources. Studies the author did not save are missing, and so are null results that were never published.
- Extraction used targeted full-text passages. Several fields are blank where those passages did not settle them, and they need a full read.
- Five studies have coefficients with signs lost in text extraction or with reporting inconsistencies (flagged in `extraction.json`). None of those numbers is quoted here.
- No risk-of-bias tool was applied. The design and rater observations above are the appraisal.

## Proposed research direction

The protocol below targets the review's central gap: outcomes rated by the employee alone. It proposes a confidential multi-wave design in which abuse is self-reported. Withdrawal is taken from HR records (absence, exits), and withholding is rated by co-workers rather than the supervisor. Recruitment must not go through the supervisor, supervisor names must never enter the analytic file, and individual responses must not be returned to the employer. The companion protocol remains a proposal. It needs population, access and ethics decisions before any data are collected.

# Paper 9 — Empirical protocol v2: Abusive supervision: silence, withdrawal and harm measured separately

> **Status: PROPOSAL awaiting AMET University Institutional Ethics Committee (IEC) approval.** No data have been collected; no results exist. Sample sizes are computed from **assumed** smallest effects of interest, not from any study. Instruments are ScaleScope catalogue entries whose source articles were resolved on Crossref (9 October 2026). Version 2 replaces the v1 draft `paper-9-oct-2024-protocol.md`.

## 1. Research question
Is earlier perceived abusive supervision associated with later defensive silence, withdrawal and counterproductive behaviour, rated by different sources?

## 2. Hypotheses (to be pre-registered)
- H1: Earlier abusive supervision predicts later defensive silence, controlling for baseline silence.
- H2: The association with withdrawal holds for HR-recorded absence where available.
- H3: Effects on counterproductive behaviour are target-specific (supervisor- vs organisation-directed).

## 3. Design
Three-wave survey (3 months apart); co-worker reports where consented; no recruitment through supervisors.

**Measurement occasions**
- T1: abusive supervision, baseline outcomes
- T2 (3 months): silence, withdrawal
- T3 (6 months): CWB, voice

## 4. Population, eligibility and recruitment
**Population(s):** a paid online research panel (Indian working adults); working professionals in India (organisations reached through alumni, professional networks and recruiter contacts).

**Eligibility:** Employed adults (18+) with an identifiable direct supervisor for 6+ months. Exclusion: failing two or more embedded attention checks; incomplete primary measures at the analysed wave (handled under §8).

**Recruitment and independence safeguards**
- **Paid online panel** — a commercial panel provider (to be selected; must allow India-resident adult workers, pre-screening on eligibility, attention checks and payment at or above the provider's fair-pay guidance). Prescreen answers are re-asked inside the survey for verification.
- **Working professionals in India** — via alumni networks, professional associations and LinkedIn posts; where organisational data (HR records, supervisor ratings) are needed, a signed **organisational access letter / data-sharing agreement** is obtained first and the organisation never sees individual responses.

## 5. Measures
| Construct | Instrument (ScaleScope id) | Items | Occasion | Source article (Crossref-verified) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abusive supervision | Abusive Supervision Scale (ASS, #15) | 15 | T1, T3 | [10.2307/1556375](https://doi.org/10.2307/1556375) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Defensive silence | Employee silence motives — defensive dimension (outside catalogue) | see source | T1, T2; defensive-silence-motive dimension | [10.1002/job.1829](https://doi.org/10.1002/job.1829) | confirm permission/licence; measure confirmed in title/abstract |
| Turnover intention (withdrawal) | Turnover Intention Scale (TIS, #7) | 3 | T2 | [10.1037/0021-9010.63.4.408](https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.63.4.408) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Counterproductive work behaviour | Counterproductive Work Behavior Scale (CWB-C, #92) | 19 | T3, self and co-worker | [10.1037/0021-9010.85.3.349](https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.85.3.349) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |
| Voice behaviour | Voice Behavior Scale (VBS, #94) | 6 | T3 | [10.1037/0021-9010.83.6.853](https://doi.org/10.1037/0021-9010.83.6.853) | confirm permission/licence with copyright holder |

All instruments are administered in English (the working language of the target population). Any translation or wording adaptation (e.g. day-level or target-shifted versions) is labelled **adapted — not validated**, piloted with cognitive interviews (n ≈ 10) and checked for factor structure before the main study.

## 6. Sample size
Noncentral-F test of 1 predictor(s) within 4: f² = 0.02 needs **395** completers (80% power, α = .05). With assumed attrition/exclusion of 35% across waves, recruit **608**. *Assumption:* Lagged effect with baseline control, f² = .02.

Target completers: **395**; recruitment target: **608**. Power will be re-checked by simulation with pilot variances before pre-registration; if the target is not reachable, the study is reported as estimation (confidence intervals) rather than as a confirmatory test.

## 7. Procedure and timing
1. IEC approval → OSF pre-registration (hypotheses, analysis, exclusions, stopping rule) → pilot (n ≈ 30, not analysed for hypotheses).
2. Recruitment window ≈ 6 weeks per wave; two reminders per wave; reminders stop on withdrawal.
3. Waves linked by a self-generated pseudonymous code; the linking key is stored separately from responses.
4. Data collection ends when the recruitment target is met or the pre-registered end date passes, whichever is first.

## 8. Analysis plan
Cross-lagged regression / SEM; target-specific CWB outcomes; multi-source models where co-worker reports exist.

- **Missing data:** full-information maximum likelihood (or multiple imputation, 20+ imputations) under MAR; attrition analysed against baseline variables and reported.
- **Measurement:** CFA for each multi-item measure; reliability (ω and α) reported; measurement invariance across waves/groups before comparing means or paths.
- **Inference:** two-sided α = .05; effect sizes with 95% CIs; Holm correction across the confirmatory hypothesis family; exploratory analyses labelled as such.
- **Common-method bias:** temporal separation and, where planned, other-source ratings; a marker variable is included in the survey.

## 9. Ethics (ICMR 2017 National Ethical Guidelines)
- **Risk category:** More than minimal risk — request **full committee review**. Rationale: Sensitive workplace topics (mistreatment, deviance) with possible distress and a retaliation risk if responses were linked to individuals.
- **Consent:** written/electronic informed consent before any question; separate consent items for each optional element (record linkage, co-worker/supervisor contact, follow-up waves).
- **Voluntariness:** no penalty for non-participation or withdrawal; no data from or to supervisors/appraisers at individual level.
- **Confidentiality & data protection:** pseudonymised data, linking key held only by the PI on an encrypted drive; processing consistent with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023; retention 5 years after publication (or as the IEC directs), then deletion.
- **Support:** debrief page with the national tele-mental-health helpline (Tele-MANAS, 14416 — verify before use) and contact details of the PI and IEC.
- Ethics pack (IEC application summary, participant information sheet, consent form, debrief): `../ethics/paper-9-oct-2024-ethics-pack.md`.

## 10. Open science
OSF pre-registration before data collection; de-identified data and analysis code shared on OSF after publication where consent permits (HR-record and organisational data excluded unless the organisation agrees).
